Theme

School & learning · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

Latin noun

the language

also the Latin language, in Latin, Latin lessons, Latinity

classical

Varr. LL 5.1 (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fin. 1.10: Latīnam linguam … locuplētiōrem etiam esse quam Graecam
Traupman 337

lingua Latīna

the Latin language

Cicero holds it richer than Greek (Fin. 1.10). The neuter plural Latīna, things Latin, is Latin writing or study (Cic. Arch. 23; Quint. 1.1.14).

Other words

  • sermō Latīnus — Latin speech, the Latin language

    also used · classical · Quint. 1.12.9: sermō Latīnus repugnat; Liv. 25.39.12: ex Graecō in Latīnum sermōnem (Lewis & Short); Traupman 337

  • Latīnē — in Latin

    adverb · also used · classical · Plaut. Merc. 10: eadem Latīnē Mercātor; Traupman 30; Traupman 337

    With verbs of knowing, speaking, writing and translating: Latīnē scīre, loquī, scrībere, reddere (see speak, a language). Latīnē loquī can also mean to speak correct Latin, or to speak plainly (Lewis & Short).

  • Latīnitās, Latīnitātis f. — correct Latin, Latinity; Latin as a subject

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 7.3.10: malus enim auctor Latīnitātis est; Traupman 30

    Classically pure, idiomatic Latin: Cicero follows Terence rather than Caecilius, ‘a bad authority for Latinity’ (Att. 7.3.10). Traupman’s Latin teacher is a Latīnitātis magister (p. 30).

Examples

  • nam et Latīna aliquandō īnfāns utique nūlla nōveram, et tamen advertendō didicī sine ūllō metū atque cruciātū, inter etiam blandīmenta nūtrīcum et joca adrīdentium et laetitiās adlūdentium

    for once, as a baby, I knew no Latin at all, and yet I learned it by listening, without any fear or pain, among the coaxing of nurses, the jokes of people smiling at me and the games of people playing with meAug. Conf. 1.14.23

  • nōn longē itaque Latīna subsequī dēbent et citō pariter īre

    so Latin should follow not far behind, and soon the two should go side by sideQuint. 1.1.14
